items.followUp: If 12 cm³ of ethanol is used to prepare 150 cm³ of aqueous solution, calculate the percentage concentration by volume.

rubric.why: Award for identifying the volume of acetone and the final solution volume.
rubric.how: Look for 5 cm³ acetone and 90 cm³ solution.

rubric.why: Award for choosing the volume-by-volume percentage formula.
rubric.description: Uses the correct formula for percentage concentration by volume.
rubric.how: Look for volume of solute divided by volume of solution, multiplied by 100.

rubric.why: Award for correct substitution of the given volumes into the formula.
Award for the correctly calculated percentage, allowing rounding.
rubric.description: Gives the percentage concentration with a percent sign.

modelAnswer: Given: Volume of acetone = 5 cm³ = 5 × 10⁻⁶ m³; volume of solution = 90 cm³ = 9 × 10⁻⁵ m³.
Formula: Percentage concentration by volume = (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100.
Answer: The aqueous solution has a concentration of 5.56% (v/v).

items.followUp: Define one atomic mass unit and give its value in grams.

rubric.why: Award for the defining reference used for the atomic mass unit.
rubric.description: Defines the atomic mass unit relative to carbon-12.
rubric.how: Look for one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

rubric.why: Award for the approximate value in grams.
rubric.description: States the value of one atomic mass unit in grams.

modelAnswer: One atomic mass unit (u) is one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.

items.followUp: The empirical formula of a compound is CH₂O and its molecular mass is 180 u. Find its molecular formula.

rubric.why: Award for the correct multiplier relationship.
rubric.description: States how to find the multiplier from the molecular and empirical formula masses.
rubric.how: Look for n = molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass.

rubric.why: Award for explaining how the multiplier gives the molecular formula.
rubric.description: Explains that every empirical-formula subscript is multiplied by n.
rubric.how: Look for multiplying all empirical-formula subscripts by the multiplier.

modelAnswer: Find n = molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass.
Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n to obtain the molecular formula.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a shell and a subshell, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Award for describing a shell as a principal energy level around the nucleus.
rubric.how: Look for a shell identified as a principal or main energy level.

rubric.why: Award for distinguishing a subshell and giving an example.
rubric.description: Defines a subshell as a subdivision of a shell and gives an example.
rubric.how: Look for s, p, d or f as a subshell, such as 2p.

modelAnswer: A shell is a principal energy level around the nucleus, represented by n = 1, 2, 3, … or K, L, M, …; for example, the L shell (n = 2).
A subshell is a subdivision of a shell, represented by s, p, d or f; for example, the 2p subshell.

items.followUp: Write the electronic configuration of sulfur (S₁₆) in subshells.

rubric.why: Award for the correctly filled first subshells.
Award for the correct outer subshells and total configuration.
rubric.how: Look for 3s² 3p⁵, giving 17 electrons in total.

modelAnswer: Its electronic configuration in subshells is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵.

items.followUp: Why does atomic size generally increase from top to bottom in a group?

rubric.why: Award for noting the increase in nuclear charge across a period.
rubric.description: States that nuclear charge increases from left to right.
rubric.how: Look for an increase in the number of protons or nuclear charge.

rubric.why: Award for linking the stronger attraction in the same shell to a smaller atom.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of increased attraction on atomic size.
rubric.how: Look for electrons being added to the same shell and pulled closer to the nucleus.

modelAnswer: Across a period, the number of protons increases, so the nuclear charge increases.
The added electrons enter the same principal shell, so shielding does not increase much; the stronger attraction pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus and decreases atomic size.

items.followUp: Why does atomic size increase from top to bottom in a group?

rubric.why: Award for identifying the increased distance of the outer electron from the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus down a group.
rubric.how: Look for increased atomic radius or distance from the nucleus.

rubric.why: Award for explaining the increase in shielding and its effect on ionization energy.
rubric.description: Links extra shells and shielding to the decrease in ionization energy.
rubric.how: Look for more shells increasing shielding, so less energy is needed to remove an outer electron.

modelAnswer: Down a group, the number of electron shells increases, so the outermost electron is farther from the nucleus.
Increased shielding weakens the nucleus’s attraction to the outermost electron, so less energy is needed to remove it; therefore, ionization energy decreases.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and give one example.

rubric.why: Award for defining a chemical bond as an attractive force between atoms or ions.
rubric.how: Look for an attractive force, especially electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Award for a suitable example of a bonded substance.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a chemical bond or bonded substance.
rubric.how: Look for sodium chloride (NaCl) or another valid example.

modelAnswer: A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together in a molecule or compound.
For example, the oppositely charged ions in sodium chloride (NaCl) are held together by a chemical bond.
